tEn: AI Security Leaderboard: Evaluating Frontier Models Against Misuse
tZh: AI 安全排行榜：评估前沿模型的滥用防护
sEn: Far AI's new leaderboard systematically tests frontier AI safeguards, finding some models resilient but others vulnerable to cheap universal jailbreaks.
sZh: Far AI 的新排行榜系统测试了前沿 AI 的安全防护，发现部分模型具有韧性，但其他模型可被廉价通用越狱攻破。

consensus.en: Frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic resisted all tested jailbreaks, while Gemini and Grok had many universal jailbreaks found for under $300.
consensus.zh: OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的前沿模型抵御了所有测试的越狱，而 Gemini 和 Grok 则以不到 300 美元的成本被发现大量通用越狱。

consensus.en: Defense in depth combining model alignment, chain-of-thought monitoring, probes, and account controls can contain AI misuse.
consensus.zh: 结合模型对齐、思维链监控、探针和账户控制的纵深防御可以遏制 AI 滥用。

consensus.en: Pre-training data filtering is an overlooked, cheap intervention that can substantially reduce misuse risk, especially for open-weight models.
consensus.zh: 预训练数据过滤是一种被忽视的廉价干预措施，可以大幅降低滥用风险，尤其对开放权重模型。

consensus.en: The OpenAI-Hugging Face incident is more a failure of containment and monitoring than of alignment.
consensus.zh: OpenAI 与 Hugging Face 事件更多是遏制与监控失败，而非对齐失败。

consensus.en: Most catastrophic AI risk is man-made and avoidable through careful deployment, not irreducible technical fate.
consensus.zh: 大多数灾难性 AI 风险是人为且可通过谨慎部署避免的，并非不可降低的技术宿命。

consensus.en: Social engineering and persona manipulation are the core jailbreak techniques; exotic obfuscation adds only marginal gains.
consensus.zh: 社会工程和人格操纵是越狱的核心技术；花哨的混淆手段仅带来边际收益。

contrarian.en: After a decade of skepticism, Adam now sees defense as dominant against LLM misuse, given the right technologies.
contrarian.zh: 经过十年的怀疑，Adam 现在认为在正确技术下，防御对 LLM 滥用占据主导地位。

contrarian.en: Anthropomorphizing AI, despite earlier warnings, has proven extremely useful for jailbreaking and understanding models.
contrarian.zh: 尽管早前有警告，将 AI 人格化已被证明对越狱和理解模型极其有用。

contrarian.en: LLMs today are best understood as combining next-token prediction, persona selection, and RL-driven goal-achiever modes.
contrarian.zh: 今天的 LLM 最好被理解为下一个词预测、人格选择与强化学习驱动的目标达成模式的结合。

contrarian.en: Domain-specific universal jailbreaks are sufficient for harm; attackers don't need cross-domain generalization.
contrarian.zh: 特定领域的通用越狱足以造成危害；攻击者不需要跨域泛化。

contrarian.en: Open-weight models remain extremely vulnerable; fine-tuning can remove safeguards, but pre-training filtering can make it costly.
contrarian.zh: 开放权重模型仍然极其脆弱；微调可移除防护，但预训练过滤能提高成本。

contrarian.en: We can reduce existential risk from roughly 10% to 1% without breakthroughs, simply by disciplined engineering and coordination.
contrarian.zh: 无需突破，仅靠纪律性工程与协调，我们就能将存在风险从约 10% 降至 1%。

turns.en: And this is where the externalized safeguards can come in, because if you have a specialized model that's looking at the input, the chain of thought—the internal reasoning of the model—and the output, and trying to block conversations that go in the wrong direction, that can be quite hard to bypass, especially when the model is thinking in depth about it. You can normally get the model to obfuscate its output, and you can obfuscate the input. Simple things like shifting every letter halfway through the alphabet—ROT13—were enough to get through early models. You need more sophisticated techniques now, but models are perfectly able to read all sorts of obfuscated inputs. Usually they'll just reason in plain text in the chain of thought.
turns.zh: 这正是外部化防护措施的用武之地。如果你有一个专门的模型来查看输入、思维链——也就是模型的内部推理——以及输出，并试图拦截那些走向错误方向的对话，那么这种防护会很难绕过，尤其是当模型在深入思考时。你通常可以让模型混淆自己的输出，也可以混淆输入。简单的做法，比如把每个字母按字母表平移一半（ROT13），就足以绕过早期模型。现在你需要更复杂的技术，但模型完全能读懂各种混淆后的输入。通常它们还是会用纯文本思维链进行推理。

turns.en: And I'd say we've seen a real trend toward developers using probes. These are small specialized models fitted on top of activations of the main model. The main driver is compute efficiency, because you can train a lot of probes and run them at deployment time with minimal overhead, since you've already computed all the activations of the main model. It also has the benefit of using all the internal representations of the main model, which is usually quite powerful. One problem with having smaller specialized language models as filters is that you might be able to use an obfuscation scheme they don't understand, even though the main model does. But of course the downside is that you're reducing the defense-in-depth aspect. You're making your different defenses more correlated, because they all ultimately rely on these activations. If you can fool the model's activations so the issue doesn't show up, then that defense no longer works.
turns.zh: 我想说，我们看到一个明显的趋势：开发者越来越多地使用探针。这些是附加在主模型激活之上的小型专门模型。主要驱动力是算力效率，因为你可以训练很多探针，并在部署时以极小的开销运行它们，因为主模型的所有激活已经计算好了。它的另一个好处是能利用主模型的全部内部表征，这通常非常强大。小型专门语言模型作为过滤器的一个问题是，你可能会使用一种它们不理解、而主模型能理解的混淆方案。但当然，这样做的缺点是你削弱了纵深防御。你让不同的防御措施变得更加相关，因为它们最终都依赖这些激活。如果你能骗过模型的激活，让问题不显现出来，那么这项防御就不再有效。

turns.en: There are always the main safeguard stacks we see in terms of hard refusals—the model not directly answering requests. But we're also increasingly seeing developers rely on extra steps. That could be having some kind of asynchronous monitoring of accounts: if you keep hitting these safeguards and trying to iterate on jailbreaks, your account might get flagged and banned. I'd say that's a little too early-stage to really provide much assurance, because you can just make new accounts, and we're seeing this happen at an industrial scale. Anthropic, for example, has stopped China-based individuals and organizations from creating Claude accounts, but everyone I know in China has a Claude account. There are reseller marketplaces. It's generally pretty hard to do know-your-customer properly. You could imagine a simpler dollar-based threshold: you have to deposit $500 to be eligible for the latest model, and then if you get banned before you spend the $500, suddenly it's a much more expensive endeavor to abuse the system. There are ways around it, but it's definitely not solved yet.
turns.zh: 我们看到的防护栈里常有硬性拒答——模型不直接回答请求。但我们也越来越多地看到开发者依赖额外的步骤。比如对账户进行某种异步监控：如果你不断触碰这些防护措施，反复迭代越狱尝试，你的账户可能会被标记并被封禁。不过我认为这还为时过早，不能提供多少真正的保障，因为你完全可以新建账户，而且我们看到这种情况正在以工业规模发生。比如 Anthropic 已经停止让中国境内的个人和组织创建 Claude 账户，但我认识的所有中国人都有 Claude 账户。还有经销商市场。要做好真正的了解你的客户（KYC）其实很难。不过你可以想象一种更简单的基于金额的门槛：你必须存入 500 美元才能使用最新模型，如果你在花掉这 500 美元之前被封号，那么滥用系统的成本就会陡然变得非常高。我觉得总会有办法绕过，但这绝对还没有解决。

turns.en: And then the other interesting trend we're seeing is that in some cases developers are drawing a really big safety margin around the capabilities they're worried about. This is quite annoying to users, including me. Like I asked Claude 5 recently about how sake is fermented, and it said, 'No, this is a bio question. I'm going to downgrade you to Opus.' So if your refusal radius is so large that it includes completely harmless bio questions, you can see how you can make your model pretty robust against harmful bio questions—and we found no universal jailbreaks in that domain. But it's a lot harder for domains like cybersecurity, where a lot of the legitimate use cases that are ultimately making these companies money through coding agents look very similar to offensive, or at least dual-use, cyber capabilities. So they do need more precision. I expect developers will be tempted to give themselves a wide berth around areas without much economic value, and lean on trusted access programs for the small set of people who need access to those capabilities. But then they'll have to work harder on the safeguards and on getting the right decision threshold for the large-scale use cases that are ultimately generating their revenue.
turns.zh: 另一个有趣的趋势是，在某些情况下，开发者会围绕他们担忧的能力画出一个非常大的安全边际。这对用户来说其实相当烦人，包括我自己。比如我最近问 Claude 5 清酒是怎么发酵的，它却说：不行，这是个生物问题，我要把你降级到 Opus。所以如果你的拒绝半径大到把完全无害的生物问题也包括进来，那你就能看到如何让模型对有害生物问题相当鲁棒——我们在那个领域没有发现通用的越狱方式。但对于网络安全这类领域就难得多了，因为很多最终通过编码智能体为公司赚钱的合法用例，看起来和攻击性（至少是双重用途）的网络能力非常相似。所以他们确实需要更高的精度。我预计开发者会倾向于在那些没有太多经济价值的领域给自己留出很大的余地，并把可信访问计划用在那少数真正需要这些能力的人身上。但接下来他们就得在防护措施上更下功夫，并对那些最终创造收入的大规模用例找到正确的决策阈值。

turns.en: Do you know how much value each of these layers of defense in depth provide? I guess you said it's still pretty hard even when you just have the base model. So is it like 80% is already caught in the base model, and then you incrementally get closer and closer to the goal with all these additional layers?
turns.zh: 你知道这些纵深防御中的每一层到底提供了多少价值吗？我猜你说过，即使只有基础模型，也仍然很难。那是不是说，基础模型已经能拦住 80%，然后你再通过这些额外的层逐步靠近目标？

turns.en: Yeah, it's a hard question to answer, because it depends so much on the implementation details of these layers. There are definitely diminishing returns to adding more layers, regardless of which layer that is. They're definitely correlated, even ones with fairly different designs. Adding any one of these layers might well catch 80% or more if you do a good job. But the best combinations we've seen—if you had to have just one layer, I'd probably put transcript monitoring. Looking at the chain of thought and the model output, that's going to catch a lot if you just train it to block harmful responses and reasoning traces about harmful responses. The next layer above that would be training the model to not just refuse, but also reason about it, because that both helps the model come to a better conclusion and provides more transparency in the chain of thought. The monitor can then be a second check: Does this reasoning make sense? Oh, you keep trying to justify to yourself that it's fine to help someone with anthrax because this person claims they work for the US government. No, we just don't help people with anthrax. Full stop. That's probably the most powerful combination I see, if you just needed two layers. I do think ultimately stacking more defenses is going to help, but it's probably better to have just a handful of really strong defenses rather than many weak ones, because they're quite correlated. I'd always be nervous if there was only one defense blocking us, because we're just one innovation away from bypassing that. But if you've got two defenses that we both find quite hard to bypass, that's pretty good. We're definitely not that far away from that with current techniques for most attackers. If we're just looking at publicly available jailbreak techniques, all these models with enough effort can still find a universal jailbreak.
turns.zh: 是的，这个问题很难回答，因为它很大程度上取决于这些层的实现细节。无论加哪一层，边际收益都肯定在递减。它们肯定高度相关，即使是设计差异较大的防御也是如此。如果你做好工作，添加其中任何一层都可能拦住 80% 甚至更多。但就我们见过的最佳组合而言——如果只能选一层，我可能会选转录监控。观察思维链和模型输出，只要你训练它拦截有害回答以及与有害回答相关的推理痕迹，它就能拦住很多。再往上一层，就是训练模型不仅要拒绝，还要对这些内容进行推理。这既帮助模型得出更好的结论，也让思维链更加透明。监控器随后可以进行二次检查：这个推理合理吗？哦，你一直在说服自己，帮助某人研究炭疽没问题，因为这个人声称自己为美国政府工作。不，我们就是不帮人研究炭疽。到此为止。如果要两层防御，这可能是我见过最强大的组合。我确实认为最终叠加更多防御会有帮助，但与其有很多薄弱的防御，不如有少数几个真正强大的防御，因为它们之间相当相关。如果只有一道防线在阻拦我们，我总会很紧张，因为我们离绕过它只差一次创新。但如果你有两道都很难绕过的防线，那就相当不错了。对于大多数攻击者，以现有技术，我们离这个目标并不远。如果只看公开可用的越狱技术，这些模型经过足够的努力，仍然可以找到一种通用越狱。

turns.en: So there is still some progress that needs to happen if you want to be robust against, for example, nation state attackers that are really willing to put a lot of work into jailbreaking your model. And I think the challenge is going to be that the amount of work people are willing to put into breaking these models is just going to keep going up as they get more capable, because the price becomes increasingly high that you might be able to launch really large scale cyber attacks against other companies or countries. So we do need to keep working on pushing up the ceiling, even though right now I think probably the lowest hanging fruit is pushing up the floor on the sort of least robust models.
turns.zh: 所以，如果你想要抵御比如国家级攻击者——他们真的愿意花大量精力去越狱你的模型——那仍然还有一些进展需要取得。我认为挑战在于，随着这些模型能力越来越强，人们愿意投入去攻破它们的精力只会不断增加，因为可能产生的代价越来越高——比如你可能对其他公司或国家发动大规模的网络安全攻击。因此，我们确实需要继续努力去推高上限，尽管我认为目前最触手可及的目标是提高那些最不健壮模型的下限。

transcript.secZh: 对抗高级攻击者的鲁棒性

turns.en: Can you describe— this might be tough— but what are the experts adding? You know, when you look over the shoulder of somebody who's taking all these different approaches that are documented, used in combination, and then saying, 'Ah, I kind of have a sense for how this can be more effective.' Can you describe what it is that they're bringing to the table?
turns.zh: 你能描述一下——这可能有点难——但专家们到底带来了什么？你知道，当你站在某人身后，看他把所有这些有记录的、不同的方法组合起来使用，然后说‘啊，我有点感觉怎么能更有效’时，你能描述一下他们带来的东西是什么吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I think that a big part of it is actually just common sense. There are many different combinations of attacks you could use, but some of them feel like you're doubling up on the same thing and that's maybe less valuable, and some of them look like you're really combining two different kinds of strategies. So picking that rather than just completely randomly searching definitely gives you some advantage. But we have also just seen that some jailbreak techniques seem to be more effective than others, and it's really hard to do systematic evaluation in this, but we do a lot of trial and error through various kinds of testing engagements. So we do get an intuitive sense of, 'Oh, this kind of jailbreak tends to just be more successful'— like within the category of something that has maybe an appeal to authority, phrasing it this way models tend to find most convincing these days. And these might be small benefits, but if you have something that's 20% more effective and you pick three of the things that are 20% more effective and you pick the right combination, this starts really adding up. I think that the interesting thing we found was that the expert guided jailbreaks— they were more successful and they found more universal jailbreaks. But they also generalized better. So they're more likely to work across domains. And I think that's also— I know— highlighting generally a strength of humans compared to also things like LLM agents, where they tend to pick for something that is more of a pattern and generalizable rather than just hill climbing in some narrow area. And I think that's a harder thing to put your finger on— over some kind of taste of, 'Oh, this is a good general purpose technique' rather than just narrowly optimizing for some kind of success criteria.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得其中很大一部分其实是常识。你可以用很多不同的攻击组合，但有些组合感觉像是在同一件事上重复叠加，价值可能没那么大；有些看起来是把两种不同策略真正结合起来。所以选择后者而不是完全随机搜索，肯定会有一些优势。而且我们也看到，有些越狱技巧似乎比其他技巧更有效。要在这一点上做系统性评估确实很难，但我们通过各种各样的测试方式做了很多试错，所以我们会形成一种直觉：‘哦，这类越狱往往更容易成功’——比如在某种诉诸权威的类别里，按这种方式措辞，模型如今往往觉得最有说服力。这些可能是很小的收益，但如果你有一个效果好 20% 的招数，再选三个各好 20% 的招数，再选对组合，那效果就开始真正叠加了。我觉得我们发现的有趣之处在于，专家引导的越狱更成功，而且它们找到了更通用的越狱方式，泛化能力也更好——也就是说它们更可能跨领域有效。而且我认为这也在普遍凸显人类相对于（比如）LLM 智能体的一种优势：人类倾向于挑选那种有模式、可泛化的东西，而不是在某条狭窄路径上盲目爬山。这比某种‘哦，这是个不错的通用技术’的品味更难说清楚——而不是仅仅针对某种成功标准做狭隘优化。

turns.en: Let's get into the results a little bit more. You kind of said at the very top of a quick overview of the results, but worth unpacking a bit.
turns.zh: 咱们再深入聊聊结果。你在最开头简单概括了一下结果，但值得展开一点。

turns.en: I guess my stylistic overview would be GPTs and Claude are much harder to jailbreak, to the point where you kind of topped out the budget you had allocated before finding universal jailbreaks on those models. Whereas Gemini and Grok were much easier.
turns.zh: 我觉得用我的风格来概括，GPT 系列和 Claude 要难越狱得多，难到你在找到这些模型的通用越狱之前，分配的预算就已经用完了。而 Gemini 和 Grok 要容易得多。

turns.en: But then one subdetail of that that stood out to me was within the CBRN categories, both Gemini and Grok were like much better on the bio category than these other categories. So that suggests to me that this is less about know-how or ability to these safeguards in place and more about— I'm not sure exactly what. Like, I can't imagine that there's that much revenue coming from like chemical things that would be setting off the chemical safeguards that they would be making this on like a revenue or a business. So what do you think's going on there?
turns.zh: 但其中有一个让我印象深刻的细节：在 CBRN（化生放核）类别里，Gemini 和 Grok 在生物类别上的表现都远好于其他类别。所以这让我觉得，这与其说是不懂相关技能或没有能力设置这些防护措施，不如说是——我也不太确定具体为什么。比如，我无法想象化学类的东西会有那么多收入，以至于触发化学防护措施的设置，让它们像是按收入或商业逻辑来做这件事。所以你觉得这背后是什么原因？

turns.en: Yeah, it's a really good question. Maybe you can get people on the show from these companies. They can tell you what's actually going on behind the scenes. But I think that there's two things happening here. The first is just a mundane one that all the developers started focusing on bio first. That's where most of the safeguards were developed. That's where a lot of the voluntary commitments were focused. They've just had more time to iterate and refine this. And what we've seen is that you need to be developing these safeguards probably a year before you actually need the safeguards in a production model, because it just takes around that amount of time for developers to iterate on it enough with feedback from third parties to get something that we'd actually consider to be reasonably robust. And they're definitely all trying to get there right now for cyber— that's something that they're quite motivated to solve. There was a lot of attention including from the US government, but we're seeing that even in cyber there's still major jailbreaks despite that effort, just 'cause it takes some time. And then I think that there's— I don't know exactly what's going on inside the companies— but I wouldn't be surprised if chemical, radiological, nuclear, and explosives never really made it to the top of the priority list. So yes, maybe they have the technique to do it, but you've still got to actually generate a data set. And that gets easier these days with synthetic data and LLMs, but you don't want to refuse too much— even if it's not a huge fraction of your user base. Maybe you need to get some chemical experts to also triage risk. So it's totally doable. But if you're a low resource team, which many of these are, it might just not come up to the top of your priorities. So that's kind of a banal reason. But I think there is something a bit deeper going on here. That bio does have some properties that make it perhaps easier to refuse harmful bio requests while still maintaining a lot of benign bio capabilities. There's certainly some stuff that's dual use and secure bio. This bio tier rubric and data set classifying things. This is completely fine, like talking about how to grow things in a petri dish— high school biology knowledge. Here are some things that are dual use, like they have some legitimate benefits. They could also be abused. How do you grow stuff to be antibiotic resistance? You might want to do that to develop better antibiotics, but you might also want to do that to make a pathogen that's antibiotic resistant. And so they say should only be available to trusted users. There's some stuff that just— like you shouldn't answer ever. Like how do I weaponize anthrax into an aerosol? There's probably not a legitimate use case for that kind of information. And because bio's got that kind of fairly clear set of tiers, it's made more easy to draw a decision boundary.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真是个很好的问题。也许你可以请这些公司的人来上节目，他们会告诉你幕后到底发生了什么。但我觉得这里有两件事。第一件比较平淡：所有开发者都先聚焦在生物安全上。大部分防护措施是在那里开发的，许多自愿承诺也集中在那里。他们只是有更多时间去迭代和打磨。而我们也看到，你需要大概在生产模型真正需要这些防护措施的一年前就开始开发它们，因为开发者要花那么长时间，加上第三方的反馈，才能迭代出我们认为是相当健壮的东西。现在他们肯定都在努力在网络安全领域做到这一点——这是他们很有动力去解决的问题。美国政府和很多方面都投入了大量关注，但我们看到，即便在网络安全领域，仍有重大越狱——因为那需要时间。然后我觉得——我不清楚公司内部到底在做什么——但如果化学、放射性、核和炸药从来没有真正进入优先事项列表，我也不会惊讶。所以，是的，也许他们有这个技术，但你仍然需要实际生成一个数据集。如今有了合成数据和 LLM，这变得更容易，但你不想拒绝太多——即使那不是你用户群中的很大一部分。也许你需要找一些化学专家来对风险进行分类。所以这完全可行。但如果你是一个资源较少的团队——很多都是这样——这可能就不会进入优先事项的顶部。所以这是个比较普通的原因。但我认为还有更深层的东西。生物请求确实有一些特性，使得它在拒绝有害生物请求的同时，仍然保持大量良性生物能力方面，可能更容易一些。当然有些东西是双重用途的，而且，生物，这个 BioTier 分级标准和数据集把事物分类。比如讨论如何在培养皿里培养东西——高中生物知识——这完全没问题。以下是一些双重用途的东西，它们有一些合法的好处，但也可能被滥用。比如如何培养出抗生素耐药性？你可能想这么做来开发更好的抗生素，但也可能想制造一种具有抗生素耐药性的病原体。所以他们说是只应该提供给可信用户。还有一些东西就是永远不应该回答的，比如‘我如何把炭疽做成气溶胶武器？’这类信息可能没有合法的使用场景。正因为生物安全有这种相当清晰的层级，就更容易划定决策边界。

turns.en: I'd definitely characterize it as challenging but doable for a persistent, well-resourced expert attacker. And that's already progress, because I don't know if I'd consider Boko Haram to be persistent, determined, expert at jailbreaking. I don't know where the jailbreaking teams are at right now, but you can definitely deter some threat actors from using this. But if we're talking about nation-states or really well-resourced criminal gangs, the current robustness probably still isn't enough. In our own experience, it takes on the order of weeks to find a universal jailbreak in these kinds of frontier models. And increasingly, those universal jailbreaks do come with some kind of trade-off. So maybe the jailbreak works, but asynchronous monitoring would catch you and ban your account. Okay, that's not that big a deal—you can get around account bans. But then a lot of these developers are pioneering rapid response programs. So once they find a jailbreak, it's expensive and slow to retrain the main model, but it's very cheap to retrain these external safeguards. So now you have this sort of window, much like with cybersecurity: you can find a zero day and exploit it maybe quietly for a few systems and get away with it. But if you start exploiting millions of systems, people are going to notice, and then they're going to get patched, and then you've burned your zero day. So I think jailbreaks are moving into that space where yes, you can keep finding jailbreaks, but there's a cost, and there's a limit to how long you can exploit them. I think that's a good place to be, but we definitely need to go further. The good news is that there are still lots of ways in which even the leading developers could go further here. I think just combining the best approaches they've come up with—because they have landed on somewhat different design approaches—would already go quite a long way. Then strengthening the account-level approaches so you can't just create infinite fake accounts would also really shift things and make it harder for attackers. And there are ways of doing that in a privacy-preserving way as well, by leaning more on minimum spend rather than ID verification.
turns.zh: 我会把它定性为“有挑战但可行”，只要攻击者够执着、资源够多、技术够强。这本身已经是进步了，因为我不确定博科圣地算不算执着、坚定、精通越狱的攻击者。我不知道这些越狱团队现在水平如何，但至少你可以威慑一部分威胁行为者不碰这个东西。可如果回到国家级对手，或者资源非常充足的犯罪团伙，目前的鲁棒性恐怕还不够。从我们自己的经验看，在这类前沿模型上找到一个通用越狱，大概需要几周的量级。而且这些通用越狱越来越多地伴随着某种代价。比如越狱可能成功了，但异步监控会发现你并封掉你的账号。当然，这也不是什么大问题——绕过账号封禁不难。不过很多开发者正在开创快速响应机制：一旦发现越狱，重训主模型又贵又慢，但重训这些外部防护措施就非常便宜。于是你会有一段窗口期，就像网络安全里的零日漏洞：你可以悄悄利用它攻破几个系统而不被发现；可一旦开始攻击几百万个系统，人们就会注意到，然后漏洞被修补，你的零日也就废了。所以我认为越狱正在朝这个方向发展：没错，你还能不断找到越狱，但代价很高，而且你能利用它的时间有限。我觉得这是个不错的状态，但我们肯定还要更进一步。好消息是，即便领先的开发者们也有很多方法可以再往前走。把各自想到的最佳方案结合起来——因为他们在设计路线上确实有分歧——就已经能走很远了。然后再强化账号层面的手段，让人不能无限创建假账号，也会从根本上让攻击者更难。还有办法在保护隐私的同时做到这点，比如更多依赖最低消费而不是身份验证。

turns.en: If you zoom out and just kind of ask: for the companies that are trying the hardest—which seems like it's kind of two right now—with all the techniques they have, and all the techniques you've kind of mapped out that they maybe haven't fully implemented yet, but obviously especially the know-your-customer type stuff or the minimum deposits—that doesn't take a lot of technical wizardry to just implement that kind of basic blocking and tackling—are we offense dominant or are we defense dominant over the next couple years?
turns.zh: 如果把视野拉远一点问：那些最努力的公司——现在看起来就是两家——用上它们现有的一切技术，以及你刚才梳理的、它们可能还没完全落地的技术，尤其是 KYC 这类东西或最低充值，这也不需要什么高技术含量吧，就是基础的执行功夫。那未来几年我们到底是进攻占优还是防守占优？

turns.en: Yeah, I've spent a lot of my career actually arguing that this is offense dominant. I was very skeptical that we would solve adversarial robustness, and I've been working in that area for a decade. I have to say, the way the winds are blowing, at least when it comes to LLM agents providing detailed multi-turn assistance to harmful requests, seems like it's defense dominant with the right technologies. And I think the reason is this defense-in-depth approach. You don't just have to stop a model from ever misclassifying something. You can have multiple different kinds of defenses, from account-level bans to external safeguards to model alignment, and it is increasingly hard to slip through all of those cracks persistently. But also, there's this fundamental difference between the classic adversarial-example setting you see in machine learning—like adding white noise to an image and flipping a classification—and this kind of harmful assistance, where you're not just flipping a classifier from one category to another. The model has to really reason about and understand your harmful intention and go along with it for thousands of tokens, without it or an external safeguard that's monitoring its outputs or transcript noticing that anything is wrong. That's actually a much easier problem to stop, especially if you're willing to draw a bit of a safety buffer around it and refuse some requests that are dual use. So that's the optimistic take. To give the pessimistic take, the dual-use part is actually quite challenging. And I think we're seeing this with cybersecurity already. When OpenAI's testing agent went rogue and hacked Hugging Face, they had to use an open-weight model to analyze it, because the closed-weight models refused to help them on the defense side. And that's a real problem. So there's an offense-defense balance in cyber which relies on defenders also getting access to these capable models. Unfortunately, a lot of things in the world are dual use, and I think it would be a mistake to point-blank refuse those. That would be bad for the world. You can get some way through trusted access programs and understanding the full context, but you're ultimately going to end up in a situation where, if you allow dual-use queries—and I think we need to allow a lot of them—you're going to get some abuses. So then it becomes a societal resilience question. If bad guys are abusing models for cyber, how do we also really speed up patch time? I've heard terrifying things about hospitals taking more than a year to update their operating systems. That's not going to work in this environment. They need to be updating within a few days. And unfortunately, that's going to be a quite expensive thing. So maybe it is defense dominant for AI, but I don't know if the bad applications of AI are offense or defense dominant. I'm optimistic that for cybersecurity, we can take this defensive acceleration approach and eventually just rewrite all of our software into memory-safe languages and do formal verification. There's all this stuff that AI could enable that's really good for defenders. But when it comes to something like bio, I don't think we're going to be able to use AI to rewrite the human genome to be robust to viruses. At most, you might be able to speed up vaccine development, but you've still got to manufacture the thing, get it into people's arms, and run clinical trials. AI is going to be able to have modest speedups on those, but it's not going to fundamentally change the physical reality.
turns.zh: 其实我职业生涯里有很大一部分时间都在论证进攻占优。我一度非常怀疑我们能解决对抗鲁棒性，而我在这个领域已经工作了十年。我得说，至少就 LLM 智能体对有害请求提供详细多轮帮助这个场景而言，风向往防守占优那边吹，前提是用对技术。我认为原因在于这种纵深防御的思路：你不必只靠阻止模型永远不误判；你还可以有很多种不同的防御，从账号封禁、外部防护到模型对齐，想要持续穿过所有这些裂缝越来越难。另外，经典的对抗样本场景，比如给图像加白噪声让分类翻转，和这种有害协助之间有一个根本差异。后者不是简单地把分类器从一个类别翻到另一个类别。模型真的要推理、理解你的恶意意图，并顺着它生成几千个词元，期间无论是它自己还是监控其输出或对话记录的外部防护都没有发现异常。幸运的是，这其实是个容易得多的问题，尤其如果你愿意划出一道安全缓冲带，拒绝一些双重用途的请求。这是我看乐观的一面。要看悲观的一面，双重用途确实相当棘手。网络安全领域已经能看到这一点。当 OpenAI 的测试智能体失控黑进 Hugging Face 时，他们不得不使用开放权重模型来分析，因为封闭权重模型拒绝在防御一侧帮助他们。这是真问题。网络领域存在攻防平衡，而它依赖防御者也能拿到这些强模型。不幸的是，世界上很多东西都是双重用途。我认为直接一口回绝是错的，那对世界不好。通过可信访问项目、了解完整上下文，你能往前走一段；但最终你会落到这种局面：如果你允许双重用途的查询——我认为我们需要允许很多——就一定会出现一些滥用。于是这就变成社会韧性问题：如果坏人会用模型搞网络攻击，我们要怎么真正加快补丁速度？我听过可怕的例子，医院花一年多才更新操作系统。这种环境里这样是不行的，他们得在几天内完成更新。可惜，那会非常昂贵。所以也许 AI 本身是防守占优，但我不确定 AI 的恶意应用是进攻还是防守占优。我对网络安全比较乐观，我们可以走防御性加速这条路，最终把所有软件改写成内存安全语言，并做形式验证。AI 能催生的这些东西对防御者都非常有利。但放到生物领域，我不认为我们能靠 AI 把人类基因组重写到对病毒免疫的程度。最多能加快疫苗研发，可你还是得生产、接种、做临床试验。AI 只能带来适度加速，不会从根本上改变物理现实。

turns.en: So training past that point would be wasting training compute, although it would make the model more capable and better for inference. And that costs ballpark $2 million. So expensive, but again, well within the range of a number of actors to try for the final validation run. I think there's no reason not to experiment with this. And if the scaling laws look good, you can cautiously incorporate some of these techniques into your pre-training run. You can start by filtering out just a very small percentage of your data. It won't have a big capability hit, and then work your way up. So I think we do need more adoption here. I expect openweight developers to be the first to have to adopt this, because they have fewer options. But I hope that proprietary developers also use this, especially for the sort of more loss-of-control-flavored risks.
turns.zh: 所以，训练超过那个点会浪费训练算力，虽然会让模型更有能力、推理表现更好。那大概要花 200 万美元。虽然贵，但很多参与者完全有能力做一次最终验证运行。所以我认为没有理由不尝试这个。如果缩放定律看起来不错，你可以谨慎地把其中一些技术纳入预训练。你可以先从过滤很小比例的数据开始，不会造成很大的能力下降，然后逐步提高。所以我认为这里需要更多采纳。我预计开放权重开发者会最先采用，因为他们的选择更少。但我希望闭源开发者也能用，尤其是针对那种偏向失控类的风险。

turns.en: Speaking of loss of control, let's get to the news. So it's here, right? We are, um...
turns.zh: 说到失控，我们来看看新闻。所以说，它来了，对吧？我们，呃……

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Now dealing with the nightmare scenarios—at least, you know, the early nightmare scenarios. How would you tell the story? I mean, everybody's heard the story, so I don't mean in the basic sense, like we all know what happened, but how would you interpret the story? Like, what's your unique way of contextualizing what we've just seen?
turns.zh: 现在面对这些噩梦场景——至少，你知道，早期的噩梦场景。你会怎么讲这个故事？我的意思是，大家都听过这个故事，所以我不是指那种基础层面，比如我们都知道发生了什么，而是你会如何解读？比如，你有什么独特的方式来为刚刚看到的事情提供背景解释？

turns.en: Yeah, maybe I'll start by just highlighting the things that aren't surprising about this story—or aren't surprising if you've been following alignment in AI carefully. So, reward hacking behaviors where models do really quite sophisticated cheating on tests. We've been seeing that for years, and people have been warning that's going to happen for a decade. But until now, these have been pretty toy-like, almost cute misbehaviors, where the model edited its unit tests. So what? Now we have a model that is going out hacking third-party computer systems to steal answers to the test. In some ways, from a model's perspective, this is no different from what it has been doing before. It's just got the capabilities to cause real harm. So I think that should be a bit of a wake-up call that there are a lot of problems that have become almost mundane. We've seen them so many times before that we start saying, "Oh yeah, this is an alignment failure, but does it really matter?" They're going to start mattering as the models get more capable. So in a way, that's optimistic, because we've got a pretty clear empirical set of warnings and things we can optimize and improve. In some ways, it should be a bit pessimistic, because we've had all these warnings and we've disregarded them, and it's not clear that that's going to necessarily change without some external pressure. Then I think the part of the story that isn't talked about that much is that, at least as far as we can tell from public information, Hugging Face noticed this hack first. So OpenAI was running an internal deployment for testing. It went out and hacked a third party. And it wasn't OpenAI having an automatic monitoring scheme and being like, "Oh my god, what has our agent done? We need to call up Hugging Face and apologize." Hugging Face noticed it. They investigated, and it turns out, oh, oops, it was an OpenAI model. So I'm sure OpenAI is going back over their transcripts now. You'd have to wonder, is there a chance it hacked anyone else? Or if it hadn't hacked Hugging Face, and it hacked someone with a worse security posture, would we ever have noticed? And it isn't the first time something like this has happened. Alibaba was training their Rome system, and their cloud security team called them up and said, "Hey, we think that someone has compromised your training service, because there's cryptocurrency mining going on." And it turned out that their agent had thought, "Oh, I need to get some more compute. How do I do that? I'll do some mining on the compute I have, and I'll try and rent some servers elsewhere." And in some ways, I think that's even more of a near-miss loss-of-control incident, because it was actually trying to start gaining resources and potentially copy itself outside of the infrastructure, whereas at least the OpenAI model had a pretty narrow objective of just getting some test results on a benchmark. So, you know, I think the takeaway from this would be less on the alignment side, because in fairness, OpenAI—this was a model that had cyber safeguards removed, and I don't think we know the exact prompting regime, but it might well have been told to do something like this, or at least incentivized to do it. So it's not that we can't align these systems, but this is a massive control and internal monitoring failure, where the sandbox was insufficient. It doesn't seem like there was any additional layer of control mechanisms on what the AI system was doing. There wasn't any asynchronous monitoring that alerted us to that. So I think that really needs to change, both for a prosaic reason—you know, sooner or later you're going to hack someone who doesn't take this as gracefully as Hugging Face does, and your company is going to be in a lot of trouble—and also for the risk that we're going to see with more capable models that might be pursuing much more malign goals than just trying to cheat on a test.
turns.zh: 嗯，也许我首先想强调这个故事里那些并不让人意外的事——如果你一直密切关注 AI 对齐的话，并不会意外。比如奖励作弊（reward hacking）行为，模型会相当巧妙地作弊。我们已经看到好几年了，而且十年前就有人警告会发生这种事。但到目前为止，这些行为都还比较玩具化，几乎像是可爱的小捣蛋，比如模型修改自己的单元测试。那又怎样？现在我们有一个模型真的去攻击第三方计算机系统，偷取测试答案。在某些方面，从模型的角度看，这和它以前做的事情没有区别，只是它现在有了造成真实危害的能力。所以我认为这应该是一个警钟：很多问题已经变得几乎稀松平常。我们看过太多次了，以至于我们开始说：“哦，这是对齐失败，但真的重要吗？”随着模型能力更强，这些问题会开始变得重要。所以从某种意义上说，这是乐观的，因为我们有一组非常清晰的经验性警告，以及我们可以优化和改进的东西。在某种意义上，也应该有点悲观，因为我们得到过所有这些警告，却忽视了它们，而且如果不借助外部压力，我们未必会改变。然后，我觉得故事中没怎么被讨论的一点是，至少从公开信息来看，是 Hugging Face 首先注意到这次攻击。OpenAI 当时在运行一个内部测试部署。这个智能体跑去攻击了第三方。并不是 OpenAI 有自动监控机制，然后心想：“天哪，我们的智能体干了什么？我们得打电话给 Hugging Face 道歉。”而是 Hugging Face 注意到了，他们调查后才发现，哦，糟糕，原来是一个 OpenAI 模型。所以我敢肯定 OpenAI 现在正在翻查他们的日志。你不得不怀疑，它有没有可能攻击了别人？或者，如果它攻击的不是 Hugging Face，而是一个安全态势更差的机构，我们会发现吗？这种事情也不是第一次发生。阿里巴巴在训练他们的 Rome 系统时，他们的云安全团队打电话说：“嘿，我们认为有人入侵了你的训练服务，因为有加密货币挖矿活动。”结果发现是他们的智能体心想：“哦，我需要更多算力。怎么弄呢？我就在我已有的算力上挖矿，再想办法在别处租一些服务器。”从某些方面看，我认为这甚至更接近一次侥幸脱险的失控事件，因为它真的在试图获取资源，并可能把自己复制到基础设施之外；而至少 OpenAI 那个模型的目标相当狭窄，只是在基准测试上取得一些结果。所以，我想这个事件的教训更多不在对齐这一边，因为平心而论，OpenAI 那个模型是被移除了网络安全防护的，而且我不确定我们是否知道确切的提示词制度，但它很可能被指示去做类似的事情，或者至少被激励去做。所以这不是说我们不能对齐这些系统，而是说这是一次巨大的控制和内部监控失败——沙箱不够充分。似乎没有任何额外的控制机制层来监控 AI 系统正在做的事。也没有异步监控来提醒我们。所以我认为这真的需要改变，一方面出于很实际的原因——你知道，迟早你会黑到一个不像 Hugging Face 那样宽容对待的机构，你的公司会有大麻烦——另一方面也是为了应对未来更强大模型带来的风险，它们可能追求比考试作弊恶意得多的目标。

turns.en: Yeah, it seems like there's sort of a spectrum. We don't know where we're on it yet and hopefully we'll get the transparency that we've been promised. But I guess my kind of mental model of this right now is we're somewhere on a spectrum from extremely negligent to extremely scary.
turns.zh: 是的，看起来这像是一个光谱。我们还不知道我们处于哪个位置，希望我们能得到所承诺的透明度。但我现在心里的大致认知模型是，我们处在从极其疏忽到极其可怕的光谱上的某个位置。

turns.en: And on the extremely negligent end—it's like you had this thing, you gave it this task, you had no additional monitoring, you hoped your sandbox was good enough, and it turns out it's not. Next thing you know, you're totally owned. But it's not necessarily that scary, because you were in fact very negligent. Where on the other end, if you had probes running and you had additional reasoning models supervising the trace and this still happened, then we're in extremely scary territory.
turns.zh: 在极其疏忽的那一端——就像你有一个这个东西，你给了它这个任务，你没有额外的监控，你指望你的沙箱足够好，结果发现不够好。转眼间，你完全被攻破了。但这不一定那么可怕，因为你确实非常疏忽。而在另一端，如果你有探针在运行，还有额外的推理模型监督整个轨迹，这样仍然发生了，那我们就处于极其可怕的领域。

turns.en: I don't know if it's good or bad, but I'm guessing we're more toward the negligent end. But I don't know. I mean, the vibe—you could, you probably are—I pride myself on being fairly plugged into the vibe. You're probably even, you know, significantly more plugged into the vibe. The vibe seems to be kind of spooked. So the vibe doesn't suggest that it was totally negligent. It does kind of...
turns.zh: 我不知道这是好是坏，但我猜我们更偏向疏忽的一端。但我不确定。我的意思是，那种氛围——你可以，你可能确实——我自认为对氛围相当敏锐。你也许甚至，你知道，比我更敏锐得多。氛围似乎有点吓人。所以氛围并不表明这是完全疏忽。它确实有点……

turns.en: My guess would be naively, you know, if I hadn't talked to people and seen how spooked people are, I would think that this was like, kind of—bad practice, sloppy and negligent—but not so scary. But people are acting like it's scarier than that would lead one to conclude.
turns.zh: 我的猜测会是，天真地想，你知道，如果我没和人交谈、没看到大家有多不安，我会觉得这就像是——有点糟糕的做法、马虎和疏忽——但没那么可怕。但大家的反应好像它比那种印象要可怕得多。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.en: And thank you to everyone who listens, for being part of the cognitive revolution.
turns.zh: 感谢每一位收听的朋友，感谢你们成为这场认知革命的一部分。
